text.p: Credit Suisse First Boston, the investment banking arm of the Credit Suisse Group, said it had cut earnings estimates for ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG in light of the company's forecast for 1997.

CSFB analysts said in a research note that earnings per share (EPS) estimates for ABB AG, the Swiss parent that owns 50 percent of the ABB group, had been cut to 90 Swiss francs in 1997 from a previous estimate of 114 francs while the 1998 estimate had been cut to 117 francs from 133 francs.
CSFB, however, retained its hold rating for the shares.
On Thursday ABB disappointed markets and analysts by reporting lower-than-expected 1996 results.
Net income per share for ABB AG in 1996 fell to 85.40 francs per bearer share from 90.20 francs. The other half of ABB is owned by Sweden's ABB AB.
ABB's 1995 result was inflated by a one-off payment of $250 million from Daimler-Benz AG in connection with a transportation venture.
Excluding this gain, ABB's group net profit rose 15.8 percent to $1.233 billion. Including the gain, the 1996 profit fell 6.2 percent from 1995.
Even taking into account the one-off gain, CSFB said ABB's net and operational 1996 results had disappointed and the forecast for 1997 should lead to significant earnings reductions.
ABB on Thursday forecast that its 1997 result would "reach at least the same level as in 1996."
Ahead of the results, CSFB said the consensus forecast for ABB AG was 107 francs per share, or a rise of 24 percent.
"Obviously there is a large gap between market expectations and ABB's view," CSFB said.
CSFB noted that its own forecast for ABB in 1997 had been attached with more uncertainty than normal due to Europe's economic conditions.
"The less-than-optimistic statements by ABB regarding net profit development in 1997 confirms our view of Europe's electrical market this year," CSFB said.
